messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Vignette:
Musa was 47, a single African American man who had built his adult life around long hours outdoors as a park ranger, moving through trails, woods, and open ground with a steady competence that had once given him a sense of order. That sense changed when he was caught in a civilian war zone while traveling to visit relatives overseas, a journey he had expected to be brief and ordinary. The violence began suddenly, and in the chaos he found himself running through natural terrain that was no longer peaceful or familiar but cut through with smoke, shouting, and the sharp, swallowing light of fire. He remembered flames rising where people had been sheltering, and the sound of commands from men in military uniforms that he could not question or misunderstand. In the confusion, he did what he had to do to stay alive, and afterward he carried a private, painful conviction that the things he did in those moments did not fit the man he believed himself to be. What stayed with him most was not only that he survived, but that others did not. From the beginning he was preoccupied with the thought that he had come home when they had not, and that he had been set apart by that fact in a way that no one around him could fully understand.

When he returned to the United States, Musa noticed that certain moments brought the war back with a force that felt immediate rather than remembered. A criticism from a supervisor at work, even something as small as being corrected about the placement of signage or the timing of a route check, could leave him tense and preoccupied for hours. He was not reacting to the words themselves so much as to the feeling that he was being singled out and judged in the way he had felt under authority overseas, when a wrong move could have terrible consequences. Fire and flames had become especially potent. If he passed a controlled burn site, saw a campfire, or watched orange light flicker across a grill at a family gathering, his body seemed to brace before his mind had fully caught up. He would look away quickly, jaw tight, and find himself wanting distance from the source of the light. Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened could also unsettle him in a quieter but persistent way. As a park ranger, he could not avoid the woods, ridgelines, and open stretches of land that were his workplace, yet there were days when a trail bordered by dry brush or a stand of trees under a hot, still sky made him feel as though he had stepped back into the place where he had been trapped and afraid.

Over the months that followed, Musa began cutting himself off. He stopped answering calls from friends and let messages sit unread. Family members noticed that he no longer came by for dinners or holidays, and when he did make an appearance, he left early and kept his explanations brief. He was not trying to punish anyone; he had come to believe that he was different from them now, and that the gap between what he had lived through and what they could imagine had become too wide to bridge. He also avoided military and police uniforms or weapons whenever he could, changing his route if he saw officers gathered at a park entrance or stepping back when armed personnel were present. At work, that meant choosing tasks that kept him away from certain public areas whenever possible, though he could not always control what he encountered. He noticed that on the days when an inspection or repair took longer than expected, his mind immediately went to something having gone wrong. If a visitor was late returning from a trail, or if a radio call went unanswered for a few minutes, he assumed that something bad was happening and felt a surge of alarm that was hard to shake.

Sleep became difficult. He had trouble falling asleep and often woke during the night, alert to sounds he could not place. Even in his own home, in a neighborhood he knew well, he was unable to relax. He described feeling as though part of him was still scanning for danger, as if safety were provisional and might be withdrawn without warning. To blunt the edge of that tension, he began drinking alcohol and using medication or drugs at times when the memories, the sleeplessness, or the sense of being on guard felt unbearable. These habits did not make him feel better for long, but they became part of the way he got through evenings that otherwise felt too exposed.

By the time he sought help, Musa had been living with the combined weight of these changes long enough to see their consequences clearly. His isolation had become a pattern, and it left him feeling more separated from others than ever. He was troubled by the thought that he had violated his own values in what he did to survive, and by the guilt of being alive when others were not. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep his life arranged around avoiding reminders, staying alert, and numbing himself at night. He wanted to be able to work in the landscape he loved without feeling ambushed by it, and he was frightened that if nothing changed he would remain cut off, sleepless, and trapped in the same terrible moment.
